title: The Earthquake That Invented Modern Seismology
event_summary: On All Saints' Day 1755, a massive earthquake estimated at 8.5-9.0 magnitude struck Lisbon, followed by a tsunami and firestorm that killed between 30,000 and 50,000 people and destroyed 85% of the city. The Marquis of Pombal, Sebastião José de Carvalho e Melo, immediately sent a systematic questionnaire to every parish in Portugal asking about the earthquake's timing, aftershocks, water behavior, and building damage — creating history's first organized seismological survey. He then rebuilt Lisbon on an engineered grid with the world's first earthquake-resistant building designs, using wooden-lattice frames called 'gaiola pombalina' that soldiers tested by marching around scale models to simulate tremors.
why_forgotten: While the earthquake itself is occasionally mentioned, Pombal's revolutionary scientific response — the systematic parish questionnaires and engineered reconstruction — is rarely taught outside Portugal. His later political downfall and the Inquisition's competing narrative that the earthquake was divine punishment overshadowed the rational, data-driven response. The event also sits awkwardly between natural history and political history, falling through the cracks of both disciplines in standard curricula.
why_it_matters: Pombal's parish questionnaires established the template for every modern post-disaster scientific survey and created the empirical foundation for seismology as a discipline. His earthquake-resistant 'gaiola' construction pioneered structural engineering principles still embedded in building codes worldwide. The disaster also profoundly shaped Enlightenment philosophy — Voltaire wrote 'Candide' partly in response, and Kant wrote three treatises on the earthquake, helping shift European thought from providential to naturalistic explanations of catastrophe, a philosophical revolution that underpins modern emergency management and disaster science.
